title: Beasts and fowl: made before man, or formed after him?
summary: Genesis 1 has the fowl made on the fifth day and the beasts on the sixth, and then man. Genesis 2, as worded, has man formed, then the beasts and fowl formed and brought to him. Brenton’s Greek of 2:19 has a word the KJV lacks: God formed them “further”.
text: KJV Genesis 1:21: “and every winged fowl after his kind”. KJV 1:25: “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind”. KJV 1:27: “So God created man in his own image”. KJV 2:7: “And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground”. KJV 2:18: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him”. KJV 2:19: “And out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:19: וַיִּצֶר֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֜ים מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ [and the LORD God formed from the ground every beast of the field]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:19: Καὶ ἔπλασεν ὁ Θεὸς ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς πάντα τὰ θηρία τοῦ ἀγροῦ [and God formed further, out of the earth, all the beasts of the field]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/2/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN02.htm.
reasoning: In chapter 1 the order is fowl, then beasts, then man. In chapter 2 the sentences run: man is formed; God says it is not good for him to be alone; the beasts and fowl are formed out of the ground and brought to him. The KJV follows the Hebrew at 2:19. Brenton’s Greek adds ἔτι, “further” or “yet”, which neither the Hebrew quoted nor the KJV has.
scope: G applies at Genesis 2:19 only, for the added Greek word. The two chapters clash as worded, but they can be reconciled if chapter 2 is not telling events in order of time, or if “formed” at 2:19 looks back to an earlier forming; chapter 2 does not say either, and it numbers no days. The Greek word can be read as fitting such a reading; this record does not assert that it was meant so. No claim is made about how the two chapters came to be written. title: Arphaxad begat Salah — or Cainan, who begat Salah?
summary: In the KJV of Genesis, Arphaxad begets Salah. In the KJV of Luke, Sala is the son of Cainan, who is the son of Arphaxad. Brenton’s Greek of Genesis has Cainan between the two, as Luke does, and gives Arphaxad’s age as 135 where the KJV has 35.

Brenton Greek 11:13: Καὶ ἔζησε Καϊνᾶν ἑκατὸν καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη, καὶ ἐγέννησε τὸν Σαλά [and Cainan lived a hundred and thirty years, and begat Sala]; the KJV and the Hebrew of 11:13 have no such sentence. KJV Luke 3:35: “which was the son of Heber, which was the son of Sala”. KJV Luke 3:36: “Which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad”. Greek New Testament, Luke 3:36, TR: του καιναν του αρφαξαδ; TISCH: τοῦ Καϊνὰμ τοῦ Ἀρφαξὰδ [of Cainan (TISCH: Cainam), of Arphaxad]. title: “Until Shiloh come” — the Greek has no Shiloh
summary: The KJV has a sceptre and a lawgiver that shall not depart from Judah “until Shiloh come”, and a gathering of the people. Brenton’s Greek has a ruler and a leader, “until there come the things laid up for him”, and “the expectation of nations”.
text: KJV Genesis 49:10: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” Hebrew (WLC) 49:10, with the written and read spellings the edition prints: לֹֽא־יָס֥וּר שֵׁ֙בֶט֙ מִֽיהוּדָ֔ה וּמְחֹקֵ֖ק מִבֵּ֣ין רַגְלָ֑יו עַ֚ד כִּֽי־יָבֹ֣א [שִׁילֹה כ] (שִׁילֹ֔ו ק) וְלֹ֖ו יִקְּהַ֥ת עַמִּֽים [a sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until shiloh comes, and to him the … of peoples; “shiloh” is left untranslated because it is the word in question, and the word before “of peoples” is not glossed]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 49:10: Οὐκ ἐκλείψει ἄρχων ἐξ Ἰούδα, καὶ ἡγούμενος ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ, ἕως ἐὰν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ· καὶ αὐτὸς προσδοκία ἐθνῶν. [a ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until there come the things laid up for him; and he is the expectation of nations]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/49/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN49.htm.
reasoning: Brenton’s Greek differs from the KJV at three points in one verse. Where the KJV has the name “Shiloh” as the one who comes, the Greek has no name: what comes is “the things laid up for him”. Where the KJV has “unto him shall the gathering of the people be”, the Greek has “he is the expectation of nations”. And where the KJV has two objects, a sceptre and a lawgiver “from between his feet”, the Greek has two persons, a ruler and a leader “from his thighs”, that is, of his descent.
scope: G applies at Genesis 49:10. No H tag is proposed: the Hebrew word behind “Shiloh” is itself the matter in doubt, and nothing here shows that the KJV misrenders it. The Greek shows how one ancient translation understood the verse; it does not show what the Hebrew before its translators read, and no claim is made about which wording is original. The written and read spellings in the Hebrew edition are given for completeness only and are not the finding. Who or what Shiloh is in the KJV’s wording is a separate question and is not answered by this record. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
